content.text:
For a **typical cold**, there’s no medicine that “cures” it—colds usually get better on their own. Medicines can help **relieve symptoms**. **Antibiotics don’t help** unless a clinician diagnoses a bacterial infection. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

### Pick medicine based on your symptoms

- **Fever, headache, sore throat, body aches:**  
  **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen/naproxen** can help. Follow the label carefully, and don’t double up on acetaminophen from multiple cold products. OTC pain/fever medicines are generally safe when used as directed but can cause serious problems if overused or if you have certain conditions or take interacting medicines. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/safe-use-over-counter-pain-relievers-and-fever-reducers/best-way-take-your-over-counter-pain-reliever-seriously-four-panel-brochure?utm_source=openai))

- **Stuffy nose/congestion:**  
  Try **saline nasal spray**, steam, or a humidifier first. A **nasal decongestant spray** may help short-term, but don’t use it longer than the label says. Be cautious with decongestants if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, prostate/urination problems, or take stimulant/MAOI-type medications. Also note: the FDA has proposed removing **oral phenylephrine** from OTC products because it is not effective for nasal congestion, so check labels. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

- **Cough:**  
  **Honey** can help cough in adults and children over 1 year old; don’t give honey to babies under 1. Some people use **dextromethorphan** for a dry cough or **guaifenesin** for mucus, but avoid taking more medicines than you need. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

- **Runny nose/sneezing:**  
  An antihistamine may help, but some cause drowsiness—avoid driving or alcohol if it makes you sleepy.

### Non-medicine basics
Rest, drink fluids, use a cool-mist humidifier, saline spray/drops, and throat lozenges/cough drops if age-appropriate. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

### When to get medical care
Seek care if you have **trouble breathing**, dehydration, fever lasting **more than 4 days**, symptoms lasting **more than 10 days** without improvement, symptoms that improve then worsen again, or worsening chronic medical conditions. If you might have **flu or COVID-19**, especially if you’re high-risk, test/contact a clinician early because antivirals work best soon after symptoms start. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

If you tell me your age, main symptoms, medical conditions, and any medicines you take, I can help narrow down which OTC options are safest to consider.
